title: Graphic design: principles, colour and typography
privacy: Teacher-review draft. Practice responses stay in this tab; download them before closing. No grades or evidence-system submissions are made. Real advertisements are credited to their owners; constructed practice designs are labelled.

slides.title: Graphic design
slides.lead: Concepts → a real campaign walkthrough → your own connections → practice labs.
slides.visual:
1. Learn: elements, principles, colour, typography and delivery.
  2. Watch the thinking: analyse actual McDonald’s, Coca-Cola and Public Theater work.
  3. Connect: explain visible evidence in your own words.
  4. Practise: open selected Photoshop labs after the check.
slides.visual_alt: Learn it before you design it explained visually
slides.definition: Graphic design organises images and words so a particular audience understands a message.
slides.example: This deck teaches the vocabulary and thinking before asking you to critique or edit.
slides.narration: We will not begin by asking you to judge an advertisement without the tools to explain your judgement. First we will learn the concepts. You will see clear definitions, simple diagrams and explanations of what a decision does for a reader. Then I will walk you through real campaigns, showing how to move from a visible feature to a principle and a communication effect. Only after that model will you make your own connections and begin selected practice labs. The deck is a sequence for several lessons, not a demand to learn everything in one period.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Audience, purpose and message
slides.lead: The brief tells you what the design must accomplish.
slides.visual:
Audience — who will read it?

Purpose — what should change?

Message — what must they understand?

Action — what should they do next?
slides.visual_alt: Start with audience, purpose and message explained visually
slides.definition: A design brief states the audience, purpose, essential information, constraints and intended action. A CTA is a call to action.
slides.example: A road sign must communicate quickly at a distance. A theatre programme can support much longer reading.
slides.narration: Before choosing a colour or typeface, identify who will see the work and under what conditions. A driver passing a sign has different needs from someone studying a theatre programme. Purpose is the result you want: find a destination, attend an event, compare a product, or understand an issue. Message is the information required to achieve that purpose. The call to action names the next step. These are related but different. A beautiful layout can still fail if it hides the time, points the wrong way, or speaks to the wrong audience. We will use those questions when we reach the real billboard.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Elements are the ingredients
slides.lead: Line, shape, form, colour, value, texture, space and type.
slides.visual_alt: Elements are the ingredients explained visually
slides.definition: An element is something you can see and use. A principle describes how you organise those elements.
slides.example: A red rectangle is a shape with colour. Making it larger than surrounding shapes creates a relationship such as hierarchy.
slides.narration: Elements are the ingredients available to a designer. Line can suggest direction or separate information. Shape is a flat area. Form suggests three dimensions. Colour includes hue, saturation and lightness. Value is the lightness or darkness we perceive. Texture suggests a surface. Space is the area around and between objects. Type gives words a visible form. These ingredients do not explain the whole design on their own. We need principles to describe the relationships between them. Keep that distinction clear: a shape is an element; the way a large shape balances a smaller one is a principle.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Line and shape can guide a reader
slides.lead: A line points or divides; a shape carries a recognisable area.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><path d="M55 110H260l-35 -20m35 20l-35 20" fill="none" stroke="#137c81" stroke-width="9"/><rect x="390" y="65" width="150" height="150" rx="15" fill="#e7b04c"/><text x="55" y="270" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">LINE · direction</text><text x="350" y="270" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">SHAPE · flat area</text></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Line and shape can guide a reader explained visually
slides.definition: A line is a path or edge. A shape is a bounded, two-dimensional area.
slides.example: An arrow can suggest a route; a rectangle can contain a related information group.
slides.narration:
A line does not need to be a drawn rule. The edge of a photograph or an implied row of objects can act like a line too. It can lead the eye or divide one group from another. A shape has a recognisable boundary and occupies an area. It may be geometric, such as a rectangle, or organic, such as a leaf silhouette. We use these terms to identify what is present before judging how it works. In the billboard later, we will identify an arch-shaped fragment and explain why that particular shape can communicate a direction.

Pause for an individual response: Point to a line and a shape. What different jobs could they do in a notice?
Labelled practice feedback: A line can direct or divide; a shape can carry an area or recognisable symbol. Explain the job for the actual message.
slides.task: Point to a line and a shape. What different jobs could they do in a notice?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Point to a line and a shape. What different jobs could they do in a notice?
slides.practice_feedback: A line can direct or divide; a shape can carry an area or recognisable symbol. Explain the job for the actual message.

slides.title: Form and texture suggest physical qualities
slides.lead: Flat artwork can still suggest depth or a surface.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><circle cx="160" cy="140" r="75" fill="#247e80"/><defs><radialGradient id="sphere"><stop stop-color="#b9e7e1"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#164d50"/></radialGradient><pattern id="texture" width="15" height="15" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse"><path d="M0 0L15 15" stroke="#547d71" stroke-width="3"/></pattern></defs><circle cx="400" cy="140" r="75" fill="url(#sphere)"/><text x="70" y="265" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Flat shape</text><text x="310" y="265" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Suggested form</text><rect x="65" y="290" width="510" height="35" fill="url(#texture)"/></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Form and texture suggest physical qualities explained visually
slides.definition: Form suggests a three-dimensional object. Texture suggests how a surface might feel or look.
slides.example: Shading can make a circle appear rounded. A repeated grain can suggest paper, fabric or a rough surface.
slides.narration: Compare the flat circle with the shaded circle. The outline may be the same, but changes in value suggest that the second object has volume. That is form in a two-dimensional image. Texture is a different idea: marks, grain or visible detail can suggest a surface. Neither effect is automatically useful. A rough texture can make small text harder to read, and heavy shading can distract from an important message. Name the ingredient, then explain its job. The real LEGO illustration later uses form and texture to make small bricks feel like a much larger imagined creature.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Colour and value are different
slides.lead: Different hues can have similar lightness.
slides.visual:
Hue

Red family / blue family

Value

Light / dark
slides.visual_alt: Colour and value are different explained visually
slides.definition: Hue names the colour family. Value describes lightness or darkness.
slides.example: A pale red word and pale blue background may still be difficult to distinguish.
slides.narration: Do not use the word colour to hide which property you mean. Hue distinguishes red from blue. Value distinguishes light from dark. Two different hues can have similar value, so they may not separate strongly when used for small text. A design can therefore have an attractive hue relationship and still be hard to read. Later we will add saturation, the intensity of a colour. For now, keep the distinction between hue and value: asking for more contrast may mean changing lightness rather than replacing the entire palette.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Space and type also do visual work
slides.lead: Empty space is active; words have visible shapes.
slides.visual:
MEET HERE

Space around a message isolates it.

MEET HERE

Letterforms change its appearance.
slides.visual_alt: Space and type also do visual work explained visually
slides.definition: Space is the area between and around elements, even when it is coloured. Typography is the organisation and appearance of written language.
slides.example: A gap can separate two jobs. A typeface can make a short title feel different without changing its words.
slides.narration: Negative space does not mean white space only. A red or black area with no competing object is still space. That area can isolate a message and reduce the amount a viewer has to process. Typography includes much more than selecting a font: size, weight, line breaks, alignment and spacing all affect reading. Words are both language and visual objects. We must check what they say and how they appear. When the real billboard uses only a short phrase surrounded by a broad field, the quiet area is doing part of the communication work.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Principles organise the ingredients
slides.lead: A useful design gives elements different roles.
slides.visual:
Hierarchy: what matters first?

Alignment / proximity: what belongs together?

Balance / repetition: how do the parts belong?

Contrast / movement / scale: what relationship guides attention?
slides.visual_alt: Principles organise the ingredients explained visually
slides.definition: Principles describe relationships: hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, balance, repetition, unity, movement and proportion.
slides.example: One decision may serve several principles; making one object large can create emphasis and change the balance.
slides.narration:
Principles are not a checklist of effects to add. They help explain relationships between elements. We will teach them individually so their meanings are clear, then put them together in a real example. Hierarchy and emphasis establish importance. Contrast creates differences. Alignment and proximity organise information. Balance distributes visual weight. Repetition can create unity. Movement describes a reading path, and proportion describes relative size. You do not need to force every principle into every advertisement. A convincing explanation identifies the principles that actually help the audience understand the message.

Pause for an individual response: A red rectangle is an element. What change could create emphasis or balance?
Labelled practice feedback: Relative size, contrast or placement changes the relationship. Name the element and the principle separately.
slides.task: A red rectangle is an element. What change could create emphasis or balance?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: A red rectangle is an element. What change could create emphasis or balance?
slides.practice_feedback: Relative size, contrast or placement changes the relationship. Name the element and the principle separately.

slides.title: Hierarchy and emphasis establish importance
slides.lead: Hierarchy orders several roles; emphasis gives one role special attention.
slides.visual:
OPEN DAY
Saturday · 10 am
Tour the studios
OPEN DAY SATURDAY · 10 AM TOUR THE STUDIOS
slides.visual_alt: Hierarchy and emphasis establish importance explained visually
slides.definition: Hierarchy is the order of visual importance. Emphasis is the treatment that makes a particular element stand out.
slides.example: A larger title can lead, while smaller time and location details remain readable.
slides.narration: Hierarchy describes more than one focal point. It gives the viewer a sequence of roles: title first, useful details next, action after that. Emphasis is the specific way you make something stand out. Size, weight, colour, position or space can create emphasis. Look at the two arrangements: one establishes different roles, while the other asks every line to compete equally. Bigger is not always better. If enlarging a title hides the time or creates collisions, the decision has introduced a different communication problem. We will trace a real hierarchy rather than judge by size alone.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Contrast creates useful difference
slides.lead: Size, lightness, weight, shape and position can all contrast.
slides.visual:
READ THIS

Weak value separation

READ THIS

Stronger value separation
slides.visual_alt: Contrast creates useful difference explained visually
slides.definition: Contrast is a noticeable difference between elements. Use it to separate roles or improve recognition.
slides.example: Dark type on a pale field often separates better than pale type on the same field.
slides.narration: Contrast is not limited to colour. A thick line contrasts with a thin line, a large shape with a small shape, and a rough surface with a smooth one. The useful question is what the difference helps a viewer notice or read. In this pair, the words and background stay fixed while text lightness changes. That makes the cause easier to see. Strong contrast does not solve an unclear message or an awkward layout by itself. We will use it together with hierarchy, space and the purpose of the design.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Alignment gives the eye a dependable edge
slides.lead: Related objects share a deliberate edge or axis.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><path d="M100 40V300" stroke="#c55b25" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="8 5"/><text x="110" y="100" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="32" fill="#183443">DESIGN STUDIO</text><text x="110" y="170" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Saturday 10 am</text><text x="110" y="230" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Room 204</text></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Alignment gives the eye a dependable edge explained visually
slides.definition: Alignment connects objects through a shared edge, centre or baseline.
slides.example: A title, time and room number can share a left edge even though their sizes differ.
slides.narration: Alignment can be left, right, centred or based on another deliberate axis. The important idea is a relationship the reader can follow. Random drift forces the eye to hunt for the start of each line. A common edge reduces that uncertainty. Do not confuse alignment with making all objects identical or equally spaced. The title may be larger, and separate groups may need different gaps. Also check actual visible letter edges: a software text box can contain padding that makes numerical alignment look uneven. Optical judgment can refine a sensible grid.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Proximity groups related information
slides.lead: Near suggests together; a larger gap suggests a different job.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><text x="70" y="90" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="32" fill="#183443">DESIGN STUDIO</text><text x="70" y="125" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Explore student work</text><text x="70" y="250" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Saturday · 10 am</text><text x="70" y="285" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Room 204</text><path d="M520 72v65m0 95v65" stroke="#137c81" stroke-width="5"/></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Proximity groups related information explained visually
slides.definition: Proximity is grouping through distance. Related information is usually closer together than unrelated information.
slides.example: An event name and explanation form one group; time and location can form another.
slides.narration:
Spacing tells a reader which pieces belong together before they read every word. In this example, the title and explanation are near each other, while the time and room form a second group. The gap between groups is larger than the gap inside each group. That difference is the principle. There is no universal pixel number that makes proximity correct. The relationship depends on type size, content and display conditions. If essential copy feels crowded, do not automatically shrink it. Rearranging space may be the more useful repair.

Pause for an individual response: A notice needs both a shared edge and clearer information groups. Which two principles help?
Labelled practice feedback: Alignment concerns a shared edge; proximity concerns gaps that group related information. Point to where each would change.
slides.task: A notice needs both a shared edge and clearer information groups. Which two principles help?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: A notice needs both a shared edge and clearer information groups. Which two principles help?
slides.practice_feedback: Alignment concerns a shared edge; proximity concerns gaps that group related information. Point to where each would change.

slides.title: Balance distributes visual weight
slides.lead: Balance does not require a mirror image.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><rect x="60" y="65" width="220" height="185" fill="#213d4c"/><circle cx="450" cy="155" r="75" fill="#dfae4e"/><text x="65" y="310" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Different shapes can balance.</text></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Balance distributes visual weight explained visually
slides.definition: Visual weight is the attention an element attracts. Balance is how that weight is distributed across a composition.
slides.example: A smaller dark object can counter a larger pale area; objects need not have equal dimensions.
slides.narration: Visual weight can come from size, darkness, detail, colour intensity and position. Symmetrical balance uses corresponding objects on opposite sides. Asymmetrical balance uses different objects that still feel intentionally distributed. Do not treat a centred layout as automatically better. The audience and message matter. When you assess balance, identify where the weight sits and what counters it. In the real billboard, a large arch on one side and a short message on the other create a relationship that we can explain without pretending they are the same size.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Repetition creates unity
slides.lead: Repeat a rule where the roles are related.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><rect x="65" y="65" width="22" height="22" fill="#137c81"/><text x="110" y="85" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">EXPLORE</text><rect x="65" y="145" width="22" height="22" fill="#137c81"/><text x="110" y="165" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">ASK</text><rect x="65" y="225" width="22" height="22" fill="#137c81"/><text x="110" y="245" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">CREATE</text></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Repetition creates unity explained visually
slides.definition: Repetition reuses a visible treatment. Unity is the sense that the parts belong to one coherent whole.
slides.example: Matching small markers can make three related items feel like a set.
slides.narration: Repeat a treatment because the content has a relationship. Shared marker shape, colour, type style or placement can connect several items. Unity is the resulting sense that the pieces belong together. These are related but not identical: repetition is a technique; unity is a relationship across the design. Repeating everything equally can remove hierarchy. The headline and action may need different treatments because they have different jobs. In a real campaign, we can also examine repetition across several posters rather than only inside one poster.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Movement is the path through the message
slides.lead: The eye follows cues; it does not read every layout in a fixed order.
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><text x="65" y="80" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="38" fill="#183443">1 · NOTICE</text><text x="100" y="170" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#183443">2 · UNDERSTAND</text><text x="155" y="270" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="32" fill="#183443">3 · ACT</text><path d="M520 65v195l-20 -25m20 25l20 -25" fill="none" stroke="#137c81" stroke-width="6"/></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Movement is the path through the message explained visually
slides.definition: Movement describes how a composition leads the eye between elements. It can be implied by lines, position, contrast and hierarchy.
slides.example: A prominent heading can lead to supporting information and then an action.
slides.narration: A reading path is a prediction about how people may encounter a layout, not a guarantee that everyone sees it in the same order. We can suggest movement with position, contrast, direction and relative scale. A diagonal shape may lead the eye; a very large title may establish the starting point. The sensible test is to show the actual design briefly and ask what a viewer noticed. Do not invent eye-tracking results from your own opinion. Later our case analysis will distinguish a plausible reading path from a measured audience response.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Scale and proportion communicate relationships
slides.lead: Large compared with what?
slides.visual: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 350" role="img" aria-label="Authored explanatory diagram"><rect width="640" height="350" fill="white"/><circle cx="180" cy="150" r="95" fill="#137c81"/><circle cx="435" cy="210" r="25" fill="#d5a547"/><text x="95" y="315" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#183443">Relative size creates meaning.</text></svg>
slides.visual_alt: Scale and proportion communicate relationships explained visually
slides.definition: Scale is size relative to a reference or context. Proportion is the size relationship between parts.
slides.example: A huge imagined object beside a tiny object can suggest transformation or imagination.
slides.narration:
Absolute dimensions do not explain every effect. A shape can feel enormous because another shape provides a small reference. Proportion describes how the parts compare with each other. Designers use those relationships to establish importance or communicate an idea. This is different from merely increasing resolution or enlarging every element. In our later LEGO example, the relationship between the large imagined creature and the small construction is central to the message. We must first learn the terms so that explanation is more precise than saying the image looks cool.

Pause for an individual response: How could relative size create a focal point but also make a notice fail?
Labelled practice feedback: A larger headline may create emphasis but can crowd the date or action. Test whether the required message still reads.
slides.task: How could relative size create a focal point but also make a notice fail?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: How could relative size create a focal point but also make a notice fail?
slides.practice_feedback: A larger headline may create emphasis but can crowd the date or action. Test whether the required message still reads.

slides.title: Hue, saturation and value describe a colour
slides.lead: Family · intensity · lightness.
slides.visual_alt: Hue, saturation and value describe a colour explained visually
slides.definition: Hue is the colour family. Saturation is its intensity. Value is its perceived lightness or darkness.
slides.example: You can keep a blue hue while making it more muted or darker.
slides.narration: When a colour decision fails, identify the property you need to change. Hue answers which colour family. Saturation answers how intense or muted it is. Value answers how light or dark it appears. They are useful design distinctions, though different software models encode them in different ways. A muted palette can still have strong light-dark contrast; a bright palette can still make text difficult to read. Avoid universal statements that a particular hue always creates one emotion. Audience, surrounding colours, cultural context and the content change how a palette is interpreted.
slides.source: Adobe: colour modes; traditional RYB relationships are labelled teaching diagrams
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Colour models
slides.lead: RGB light, CMYK printing and an RYB teaching wheel have different purposes.
slides.visual:
RGB / CMYK

RGB mixes light for screens.

CMYK uses process inks for printing.

Traditional RYB wheel

An artist’s hue-relationship model.

Its opposites are not RGB complements.
slides.visual_alt: Name the colour model explained visually
slides.definition: A colour model describes a way of organising or specifying colour. The model determines what an opposite or primary means.
slides.example: Blue and orange are opposite on our traditional RYB wheel; blue and yellow are additive RGB complements.
slides.narration: Do not combine colour models without saying so. Screens use red, green and blue light. Process printing commonly uses cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks. The traditional artist’s wheel uses red, yellow and blue as its teaching primaries. These models do not have identical mixtures or opposites. We will use a labelled RYB wheel to discuss traditional palette relationships, and actual screen colour pairs to discuss readability. When preparing a real delivery file, use the destination’s colour-management requirements rather than assuming that the teaching wheel predicts printed colours.
slides.source: Adobe: colour modes; traditional RYB relationships are labelled teaching diagrams
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Complementary hues
slides.lead: RYB example: blue and orange.
slides.visual_alt: Complementary hues sit opposite on the named wheel explained visually
slides.definition: Complementary means opposite positions on a specified hue model.
slides.example: One hue can dominate while its complement supplies a smaller accent.
slides.narration: On this traditional RYB wheel, blue and orange are opposite. That is a complementary relationship. It describes their hue positions; it does not tell us how light, dark, saturated or extensive they should be in the design. A common useful approach gives one colour a broad role and the other a smaller accent role. That prevents equal competition for attention. Complementary colours do not guarantee readable text. We still need to inspect the actual text and background at their real size and compare lightness, not just their positions on a wheel.
slides.source: Adobe: colour modes; traditional RYB relationships are labelled teaching diagrams
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Analogous hues are neighbours
slides.lead: RYB example: blue, blue-green and green.
slides.visual: Blue → blue-green → green
slides.visual_alt: Analogous hues are neighbours explained visually
slides.definition: Analogous means neighbouring hues on a specified wheel.
slides.example: Related hues can share a family feeling while differing in lightness, area and purpose.
slides.narration:
Analogous hues sit beside one another rather than across the wheel. Our blue, blue-green and green example is a neighbouring group on the named model. The relationship can support a coherent palette, but coherence alone does not establish hierarchy. Assign different jobs and areas, and retain useful value differences. If every area has the same visual weight, the result may be difficult to read even though its hue relationship is correct. Do not diagnose a palette by atmosphere alone. Identify the actual selected hues and the roles they play.

Pause for an individual response: On the named RYB wheel, compare blue/orange with blue/blue-green/green. What is different?
Labelled practice feedback: Blue/orange are opposite hue families; the blue/blue-green/green families are neighbours. Neither relationship guarantees legible text.
slides.source: Adobe: colour modes; traditional RYB relationships are labelled teaching diagrams
slides.task: On the named RYB wheel, compare blue/orange with blue/blue-green/green. What is different?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: On the named RYB wheel, compare blue/orange with blue/blue-green/green. What is different?
slides.practice_feedback: Blue/orange are opposite hue families; the blue/blue-green/green families are neighbours. Neither relationship guarantees legible text.

slides.title: Monochromatic and triadic are other relationships
slides.lead: One hue family, or three evenly spaced hue positions.
slides.visual:
Monochromatic

Different values of blue

Triadic on RYB

Red / yellow / blue
slides.visual_alt: Monochromatic and triadic are other relationships explained visually
slides.definition: Monochromatic stays within one hue family. Triadic selects three evenly spaced positions on the named wheel.
slides.example: Neither requires giving every colour the same area or intensity.
slides.narration: Monochromatic does not mean one identical swatch everywhere. Light, dark and muted versions of one hue can create different roles. A triadic relationship selects three evenly spaced hue positions; on the traditional RYB model, red, yellow and blue are one example. These are ways to plan relationships, not formulas that guarantee good design. A neutral can carry much of the reading, and one hue can lead. Use these terms only when you can identify the relationship. A photograph containing many colours is not automatically a deliberate triadic layout palette.
slides.source: Adobe: colour modes; traditional RYB relationships are labelled teaching diagrams
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Colour roles and gradients
slides.lead: Background, information and accent are different jobs.
slides.visual:
Background supports reading.

Information remains legible.

Accent selects what needs attention.

A transition can change readability.
slides.visual_alt: Give colour a role; make a gradient useful explained visually
slides.definition: A palette assigns colours to roles. A gradient is a transition between colours or values.
slides.example: Place a quieter, lighter area behind dark type; inspect the weakest point when the background varies.
slides.narration: Choosing swatches is only part of a colour decision. Decide which colour supports the background, which carries information, and which is reserved for emphasis. A gradient changes across an area, so the background behind a word is not necessarily one colour. Test the least readable portion rather than an unrelated swatch. In a dark-text example, a lighter section behind the text can help. If the text becomes white, that relationship may need to reverse. A gradient is useful when it serves the message; it is not an obligatory decoration.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: A typeface has visible characteristics
slides.lead: Serif, sans serif, weight and width describe different features.
slides.visual:
Aa · Reader

Serif: finishing strokes

Aa · Reader

Sans serif: no serifs
slides.visual_alt: A typeface has visible characteristics explained visually
slides.definition: Typeface is a letterform design; font identifies a particular style/implementation. Weight is stroke thickness; width concerns letter proportions.
slides.example: Compare actual letterforms. Neither serif nor sans serif is automatically correct for an audience.
slides.narration: A serif is a finishing stroke on a letter. A sans serif design does not have those strokes. Weight describes how thick the strokes appear, and width describes a different proportion. These features can influence tone and reading, but categories do not make the decision for you. Some serif faces work well for small text and some sans serif faces do not. Compare the actual words at the intended size. Use a display treatment for a short heading only when it remains useful; body information may need a quieter treatment. We will study real expressive type after teaching its controls.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Typography needs roles and useful line breaks
slides.lead: Title, detail and action should not all compete.
slides.visual:
BIKE REPAIR TODAY
BIKE REPAIR TODAY
slides.visual_alt: Typography needs roles and useful line breaks explained visually
slides.definition: Type hierarchy assigns different jobs to text. A line break should respect the meaning and fit of a phrase.
slides.example: “BIKE REPAIR / TODAY” keeps the useful phrase together; another break may change how quickly it is understood.
slides.narration:
Set the roles before adding more typefaces. The title establishes the topic; details explain it; an action directs the audience. Size and weight can distinguish those roles even within one type family. Line breaks also influence meaning. Compare how the two arrangements group the phrase bike repair. The best break depends on width, size and the message, but do not let an accidental wrap decide it for you. In software, edit the line break and spacing rather than stretching letters just to fill a box. We will now distinguish three spacing controls.

Pause for an individual response: Give a headline and event details different type roles. Which visible choice would show that?
Labelled practice feedback: Use relative size/weight and suitable line breaks for different information roles. Explain the purpose rather than choosing a font only because you like it.
slides.task: Give a headline and event details different type roles. Which visible choice would show that?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Give a headline and event details different type roles. Which visible choice would show that?
slides.practice_feedback: Use relative size/weight and suitable line breaks for different information roles. Explain the purpose rather than choosing a font only because you like it.

slides.title: Kerning adjusts one letter pair
slides.lead: Pair spacing is different from spacing a whole word.
slides.visual:
AV
A V
slides.visual_alt: Kerning adjusts one letter pair explained visually
slides.definition: Kerning adjusts the space between particular characters.
slides.example: A headline may need an optical adjustment between A and V without changing every other pair.
slides.narration: Kerning concerns a specific pair of characters. Their shapes can leave an awkward-looking gap even when software spacing is mathematically consistent. In a large short title, a designer may inspect and adjust that pair. That is different from opening up every letter in a word. Do not use the terms kerning and tracking interchangeably. Automatic kerning may already produce a good result, so manual correction is not obligatory. The principle is to judge the visible pair and understand which control affects it. The sample is an authored diagram, not a screenshot of a Photoshop setting.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Tracking adjusts selected characters together
slides.lead: Spacing across a run of text.
slides.visual:
STUDY
STUDY
slides.visual_alt: Tracking adjusts selected characters together explained visually
slides.definition: Tracking changes spacing across selected letters or a text block.
slides.example: It can open or tighten a short word, but excessive tracking can fragment it.
slides.narration: Tracking changes spacing across a selected run of characters. In Photoshop, its values use thousandths of an em, not ordinary pixel gaps. Increasing tracking may make a short heading feel more open, but excessive spacing can make the letters seem disconnected. Decreasing it too far can crowd their shapes. We are comparing the same word to isolate that effect. Do not assume that the more open version is always better. The useful decision depends on actual typeface, size and context. Tracking does not directly fix a vertical collision between lines.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Leading separates text baselines
slides.lead: Vertical line spacing is different from letter spacing.
slides.visual:
Line one Line two
Line one Line two
slides.visual_alt: Leading separates text baselines explained visually
slides.definition: Leading is the distance between successive text baselines.
slides.example: Too little can crowd lines; too much can make a related paragraph fall apart.
slides.narration: Leading describes the vertical relationship between lines. A baseline is the reference line on which most letters sit. In the first sample, the lines crowd each other; the second gives them more separation. More separation is not automatically better, because related lines should still feel like one group. If a headline has a bad phrase break, changing leading alone will not repair the phrase. Diagnose the cause: pair spacing calls for kerning, group letter spacing for tracking, line spacing for leading, and wording groups for line-break changes.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Readability must be checked in the actual design
slides.lead: Hue harmony, a large title or a good font does not certify the whole layout.
slides.visual:
• Read the essential words at display size.
  • Inspect the actual text/background pair.
  • Check line breaks and spacing.
  • Check small text and changing backgrounds.
slides.visual_alt: Readability must be checked in the actual design explained visually
slides.definition: Readability depends on letterforms, size, spacing, wording, contrast and viewing conditions working together.
slides.example: Use 4.5:1 as this classroom’s conservative text-pair target, then still read the actual words.
slides.narration:
A numerical contrast check measures one relationship, not every aspect of readability. W3C distinguishes normal and large text and other requirements; our classroom uses a conservative four-and-a-half-to-one pair target as one useful check. A passing pair can still be difficult if the type is tiny, crowded or badly worded. A large title does not excuse invisible time or location information. On photos and gradients, inspect the weakest background directly behind the letters. We will apply these checks to real designs without claiming that our discussion is a complete accessibility audit.

Pause for an individual response: Two lines are crowded vertically, but the letters within each word are fine. Which spacing changes?
Labelled practice feedback: Leading changes baseline distance. Tracking spreads a selected run; kerning changes one pair. Check the actual mismatch.
slides.task: Two lines are crowded vertically, but the letters within each word are fine. Which spacing changes?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Two lines are crowded vertically, but the letters within each word are fine. Which spacing changes?
slides.practice_feedback: Leading changes baseline distance. Tracking spreads a selected run; kerning changes one pair. Check the actual mismatch.

slides.title: Images and words must support the same message
slides.lead: An attractive image can still communicate the wrong thing.
slides.visual:
Words: what information is promised?

Image: what story is suggested?

Together: do they support the actual brief?
slides.visual_alt: Images and words must support the same message explained visually
slides.definition: Composition organises the elements into one communication. Audience fit means the decisions serve the intended people and purpose.
slides.example: An image can supply an idea while a short line clarifies the action. Neither should contradict the brief.
slides.narration: A design can be technically tidy while its message is wrong. Compare what the words promise with what the image suggests. If they disagree, the audience may misunderstand the offer or purpose. That is why critique must refer to the brief rather than a personal preference. We can describe evidence we see and an interpretation of its likely effect; we should not invent audience research to prove the interpretation. The real campaigns will show different ways images and words cooperate. Their approaches are useful examples, not templates to copy onto every client.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Editable masters and exported images
slides.lead: Editable source and viewing copy have different jobs.
slides.visual:
Layered PSD

Editable text, objects and effects.

Retain for revisions.

PNG / JPEG

Raster viewing copies.

Reopen and inspect actual files.
slides.visual_alt: Keep the master; inspect the delivered file explained visually
slides.definition: The master preserves editing. An export is a delivery file for a specified destination.
slides.example: PNG uses lossless image compression and can retain transparency. JPEG usually trades detail for smaller photo files.
slides.narration: A screenshot of export settings is not the delivered result. Keep the layered master, export a separate viewing file, and reopen that actual file. PNG preserves its encoded pixels without lossy compression and can retain transparency. JPEG usually uses lossy compression and can produce visible artefacts, especially near lettering. Which is more useful depends on content and requirements; compare real files rather than guess. Do not overwrite the only layered source to obtain a smaller delivery file. File dimensions, colour handling and output inspection are part of the communication job.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Pixels, PPI and colour space are different
slides.lead: Changing a PPI label alone does not add image detail.
slides.visual:
Pixels: the stored image grid.

PPI: a relationship to physical print size.

sRGB: common colour space for screen delivery.
slides.visual_alt: Pixels, PPI and colour space are different explained visually
slides.definition: Pixel dimensions measure image width and height. PPI metadata relates pixels to physical size. A colour space defines colour interpretation.
slides.example: A 1080×1350 image keeps that pixel grid when only its PPI metadata changes.
slides.narration: The stored pixel grid and physical print scale are different quantities. If an image has too few pixels for the requested display, changing only its PPI tag does not create missing detail. Re-export from an appropriate master. Colour space is another separate requirement: screen delivery commonly uses sRGB, while print specifications depend on the destination. Record the actual requirements and inspect exported files. These concepts prepare you for the export lab, but we are still learning before beginning it. We have now taught the foundation vocabulary and can use it in a real campaign walkthrough.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Design reference map
slides.lead: Ingredient → relationship → communication effect.
slides.visual:
Elements: line, shape, form, colour/value, texture, space, type.

Principles: hierarchy/emphasis, contrast, alignment, proximity, balance, repetition/unity, movement, scale/proportion.

Controls: hue/saturation/value; palette roles; typeface/weight; kerning/tracking/leading; delivery choices.
slides.visual_alt: Keep this map beside the real examples explained visually
slides.definition: A strong explanation names something visible, the relationship it creates, and why that matters for the audience.
slides.example: “A large yellow curve balances the smaller white message” is more specific than “the design looks good”.
slides.narration:
We have finished the teaching section. Keep this map as a reference while I model the analysis. Start with an ingredient you can point to, then name the relationship it creates, then explain the communication effect. Avoid listing every term without evidence. If a concept is not visible or cannot be checked from the source, say so. We will look at a road billboard, a recycling campaign and an expressive theatre poster. Each has a different purpose, so a decision that helps one may be inappropriate for another. Your own connection tasks come after the walkthrough.

Pause for an individual response: Two exported images both have 1080 × 1350 pixels; one says 72 PPI and one 300 PPI. Which has more pixels?
Labelled practice feedback: Neither: both have the same pixel dimensions. PPI metadata affects print interpretation; it does not add pixels or prove screen clarity.
slides.task: Two exported images both have 1080 × 1350 pixels; one says 72 PPI and one 300 PPI. Which has more pixels?
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Two exported images both have 1080 × 1350 pixels; one says 72 PPI and one 300 PPI. Which has more pixels?
slides.practice_feedback: Neither: both have the same pixel dimensions. PPI metadata affects print interpretation; it does not add pixels or prove screen clarity.

slides.title: Real example: Follow the Arches
slides.lead: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette, 2018. A roadside directional billboard.
slides.visual_alt: Real example: Follow the Arches explained visually
slides.definition: Brief first: help a passing viewer recognise the brand and understand the directional message.
slides.example: Cossette describes the campaign as using deconstructed arches for directional billboards. This photograph supplies the visible evidence.
slides.narration: We will analyse this real billboard in order. First establish purpose and viewing conditions. Cossette identifies the campaign as directional outdoor advertising for McDonald’s Canada. A roadside viewer has limited reading time. The photographed board uses a short phrase and a fragment of the familiar arch rather than a menu or a detailed story. The agency’s description supports the directional purpose. Our next observations about hierarchy and balance are design analysis based on the visible image, not measured proof that every driver read it successfully. Notice how little content the board asks the viewer to process.
slides.source: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette · Follow the Arches · 2018
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Walkthrough 1: identify the elements
slides.lead: Name what is visible before explaining its effect.
slides.visual: Teaching overlay on the unchanged source photograph.
slides.visual_alt: Walkthrough 1: identify the elements explained visually
slides.definition: Visible evidence: a broad red field, a cropped yellow curve, short white type and a large quiet area.
slides.example: The curve is a shape; the field and words use colour/value; the unused area is space; the phrase is type.
slides.narration: I begin with observations rather than a verdict. I can point to a broad red field, a large yellow curved fragment on the right, and a short white phrase toward the left. The curve is a flat shape. The photograph shows a physical billboard, but the graphic on its face is deliberately simple. The open field around the phrase is space, even though it is red. The words are type and their exact message matters. I do not need to call every ingredient a principle. Once those visible parts are identified, I can explain their relationships on the next slide.
slides.source: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette · Follow the Arches · 2018
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Walkthrough 2: explain hierarchy and contrast
slides.lead: Different sizes and values give the two main parts different roles.
slides.visual: Teaching overlay on the unchanged source photograph.
slides.visual_alt: Walkthrough 2: explain hierarchy and contrast explained visually
slides.definition: The large curve supplies recognition and direction; the smaller phrase clarifies the situation.
slides.example: Yellow and white stand out from the broad red field. This is a visible separation, not a completed contrast-ratio audit.
slides.narration: The yellow curve occupies much more area than the words, so it is a plausible first recognition cue. The short phrase gives information the curve cannot state alone. Their contrast comes from size, colour and value against the red field. I can explain those differences without pretending I measured exact brand colours from a compressed photograph. Nor can I claim a universal first-read order. My model is a plausible explanation: recognition cue, clarifying words, directional meaning. A useful test would show the image briefly to viewers and ask what they understood, without telling them the expected answer.
slides.source: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette · Follow the Arches · 2018
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Walkthrough 3: connect balance and space
slides.lead: A large shape on one side can balance a smaller message on the other.
slides.visual_alt: Walkthrough 3: connect balance and space explained visually
slides.definition: The composition is asymmetrical: its left and right sides have different shapes and areas.
slides.example: The quiet red area isolates the phrase; the large right-hand curve counters its placement.
slides.narration:
Balance does not require duplicating the arch on the left. The large curve and the smaller white phrase occupy different sides, creating an asymmetrical relationship. The quiet red field isolates both rather than filling every gap with information. My analysis connects that space to the viewing condition: less competition can help a passing viewer find the main cues. It is an inference about communication, not a reported performance result. If I added a product photo, a price list and extra icons, I would create new competing roles. The extra content might be useful in another format but could weaken this particular directional purpose.

Pause for an individual response: Point to one visible billboard feature and explain its purpose for a passing viewer. Name one limitation.
Labelled practice feedback: Connect a visible feature to hierarchy, contrast, balance or space and the quick encounter. Recognition depends on prior brand knowledge; the photograph does not measure effectiveness.
slides.source: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette · Follow the Arches · 2018
slides.task: Point to one visible billboard feature and explain its purpose for a passing viewer. Name one limitation.
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Point to one visible billboard feature and explain its purpose for a passing viewer. Name one limitation.
slides.practice_feedback: Connect a visible feature to hierarchy, contrast, balance or space and the quick encounter. Recognition depends on prior brand knowledge; the photograph does not measure effectiveness.

slides.title: Walkthrough 4: build the complete explanation
slides.lead: Visible feature → principle → audience effect → limitation.
slides.visual:
1. Feature: a large cropped arch and short phrase.
  2. Principles: contrast, hierarchy, asymmetrical balance and space.
  3. Effect: fast recognition with a clarifying directional message.
  4. Limit: it relies on familiarity with the brand; a new café cannot assume that.
slides.visual_alt: Walkthrough 4: build the complete explanation explained visually
slides.definition: A reasoned explanation connects the design decision to the purpose, rather than praising a style.
slides.example: This is the teacher’s complete model. Your later response should use its reasoning pattern with your own evidence.
slides.narration: Now I combine the observations. The large cropped arch uses familiarity with an established brand, while the short white phrase clarifies the directional situation. Contrast and space separate the main cues; asymmetrical balance organises them without requiring symmetry. Those choices suit a fast roadside message. The limitation is important: the method depends on prior recognition. An unfamiliar café cannot assume that a cropped fragment identifies it. Notice how the explanation goes beyond naming terms, but stays within the evidence. I am not claiming sales results or safe driving outcomes. I am explaining the communication design and a condition that could make it fail.
slides.source: McDonald’s Canada / Cossette · Follow the Arches · 2018
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Real example: Recycle Me
slides.lead: Coca-Cola / WPP Open X, led by Ogilvy New York.
slides.visual_alt: Real example: Recycle Me explained visually
slides.definition: The agency describes crushed-can logo variations and a recycling call to action.
slides.example: The series repeats red fields, white marks and a small action line. The centre changes; the surrounding system remains recognisable.
slides.narration: This second real example has a different purpose. Ogilvy describes a campaign that uses logo shapes based on crushed cans and the call to action Recycle Me. Look across the three supplied executions. The broad red field and white treatment repeat, while the central mark varies. I identify the repeated rule first, then explain how it makes the posters feel like one campaign. The distorted mark contributes the visual idea; the small action line helps state the requested behaviour. The source describes intent, but this slide does not prove that people recycled more cans or that the product has a particular environmental impact.
slides.source: Coca-Cola / WPP Open X, led by Ogilvy New York · Recycle Me
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Walkthrough: colour roles, repetition and unity
slides.lead: A restricted palette can carry a campaign without a wheel formula.
slides.visual_alt: Walkthrough: colour roles, repetition and unity explained visually
slides.definition: Red carries the field; white carries the central mark and action. Similar layout positions connect the executions.
slides.example: Describe this as a restricted red/white palette. Do not invent a complementary or analogous relationship.
slides.narration: Here I connect colour to role and repetition to unity. Red occupies most of each execution, while white marks the central idea and the action. Similar positions and a repeated limited palette make the posters recognisable as a set. The variations keep the central idea from being identical in every execution. This is not a gradient example, and it is not evidence of a complementary or analogous palette. White is a neutral in our hue analysis. I should use the terms that match the actual source, not force every colour-wheel category onto it. A limitation is that tiny action text must still be checked in its intended display context.
slides.source: Coca-Cola / WPP Open X, led by Ogilvy New York · Recycle Me
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Real example: type becomes the image
slides.lead: The Public Theater / Paula Scher, Pentagram. Simpatico poster.
slides.visual_alt: Real example: type becomes the image explained visually
slides.definition: The title’s letterforms occupy much of the composition, with smaller supporting information in different treatments.
slides.example: Scale, width, weight, value contrast and placement give words expressive and informational roles.
slides.narration:
In this real theatre poster, type is both language and the main visual construction. The very large condensed black title letters dominate the surface. Red names and smaller practical information create different paths and roles. Pentagram describes The Public’s identity as an active typographic language; the exact date of this particular execution is not established here. I can analyse visible letter width and relative scale, but I cannot infer the designer’s exact Photoshop tracking settings from a printed image. This example shows expressive type in context. It does not mean every café invitation should copy its complex reading pattern.

Pause for an individual response: Which words act as a dominant visual, and which carry supporting information? Explain the difference.
Labelled practice feedback: Use the actual poster: relative width, size, weight or position can create different roles. Expressive type still needs a readability test for its intended context.
slides.source: The Public Theater / Paula Scher, Pentagram · Simpatico; execution year not verified
slides.task: Which words act as a dominant visual, and which carry supporting information? Explain the difference.
slides.success: Point to a visible feature, use the concept accurately and explain its purpose.
slides.quick_check: Which words act as a dominant visual, and which carry supporting information? Explain the difference.
slides.practice_feedback: Use the actual poster: relative width, size, weight or position can create different roles. Expressive type still needs a readability test for its intended context.

slides.title: Different purposes, different design choices
slides.lead: Road direction, recycling prompt and theatre identity are different briefs.
slides.visual:
Real casePurposeUseful design decisions
Follow the ArchesFast recognition / directionFew cues, quiet space, large recognisable shape
Recycle MePrompt an action across a campaignRepeated palette/layout, changing central mark
SimpaticoExpressive theatrical promotionTitle as image, contrasting type roles
slides.visual_alt: Compare purposes before calling a decision good explained visually
slides.definition: A principle is useful when it serves the actual audience and purpose. A real campaign can still have limitations.
slides.example: We have modelled evidence-based analysis; now you will explain your own connections.
slides.narration: We have completed the real-example walkthrough before asking you to work independently. The billboard reduces content for a fast encounter. The recycling campaign repeats a system across variations. The theatre poster uses type expressively while distributing supporting information. These are not a ranking from worst to best. They serve different briefs and each raises a different readability or recognition question. To make a connection, identify a visible feature, name the relevant concept, and explain how it helps or hinders the specific purpose. You are now ready for individual checks. We will use feedback to decide whether to reteach a concept before opening the labs.
slides.success: Name the concept, point to visible evidence, explain its communication effect.

slides.title: Connection check: choose the right concept
slides.lead: Answer individually, then explain why the other choices do not fit.
slides.visual:
Line one Line two

The letters inside each word have enough space, but the two lines collide.
slides.visual_alt: Connection check: choose the right concept explained visually
slides.definition: Use the spacing concepts you have already learned.
slides.example: Choose a control and explain what it changes.
slides.narration: This is the first independent connection check after teaching and modelling. Look at the actual problem rather than guessing a familiar term. The letters within each word are separated, but the two lines are too close vertically. Make your own choice, then explain what the control changes. Use the feedback to correct your explanation before continuing. The important evidence is your reason, not the button alone. If you still confuse the controls, return to the three definition slides and compare pair spacing, run spacing and baseline spacing.

check.correct: Leading changes baseline-to-baseline line spacing. Now explain why kerning and tracking address different gaps.
check.retry: Identify where the gap is: one pair, a run of letters or between line baselines? Revisit those definitions and try again.

slides.title: Connection check: explain the real billboard
slides.lead: Point to three visible features; connect each to a taught concept.
slides.visual_alt: Connection check: explain the real billboard explained visually
slides.definition: Use feature → concept → effect. Finish by naming one limitation or a test you would run.
slides.example: Your own explanation may differ from the model if the evidence and purpose support it.
slides.narration: You have seen the whole analysis model. Now explain the billboard in your own words. Select three visible features rather than listing every design term. For each, name a concept and explain the likely effect for a passing viewer. End with one limitation or a test. A partner should challenge one connection by asking where the evidence appears in the source. You then correct the wording or defend it. Avoid claiming measured audience behaviour from the photograph. This is a formative explanation for feedback; the design vocabulary should make your reasoning more precise.

slides.title: Connection check: transfer to a different real ad
slides.lead: LEGO / Ogilvy Bangkok; advertising illustration by Illusion CGI Studio.
slides.visual_alt: Connection check: transfer to a different real ad explained visually
slides.definition: Read the visible image and copy using the concepts taught. This is advertising illustration, not a verified photograph of a physical build.
slides.example: Choose which concepts actually explain the message; do not force every term into the answer.
slides.narration: This is a different real advertisement for your transfer check. We have not supplied a complete analysis of it. Inspect the large illustrated creature, the small construction, the quiet background and the wording at the bottom. Explain two relationships using concepts you learned earlier, then connect them to the advertised idea. Distinguish what is visible from what you infer. It would be misleading to assume the picture proves that someone physically built the exact creature. After your first response, compare with a partner and identify one place where evidence makes your explanation stronger. The teacher will review your reasoning before assigning a practice lab.
